content: Cervical cancer is the second most prevalent cancer among women under the age of 65 and remains the leading cause of death from gynecological cancers globally. Women diagnosed with stage IA2 cervical cancer, as defined by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), exhibit stromal invasion that penetrates beyond the basement membrane of the epithelium to a depth greater than 3 mm but not exceeding 5 mm. The horizontal spread of the tumor is limited to 7 mm or less. For stage IA2 cervical cancer, the standard treatment options include radical hysterectomy combined with pelvic lymphadenectomy or radiotherapy. However, given the relatively low risk of local or distant metastasis in this stage, less invasive surgical approaches may be considered to minimize complications associated with more radical procedures. These less invasive options include simple hysterectomy, simple trachelectomy, or conization, with or without pelvic lymphadenectomy. Despite this, the evidence supporting the safety and efficacy of less radical tumor excision and the necessity of systematic lymphadenectomy in stage IA2 cervical cancer remains unclear. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of less radical surgical techniques in the management of stage IA2 cervical cancer. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group trials register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to September 2013. Additional searches were performed in clinical trial registries and abstracts from scientific meetings. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different surgical techniques in women with stage IA2 cervical cancer. Two independent reviewers evaluated the identified studies for relevance. However, no trials meeting the inclusion criteria were found, and as a result, no data were available for analysis. The search strategy yielded 982 unique references, all of which were excluded based on their titles and abstracts, as they clearly did not meet the inclusion criteria. One large ongoing trial was identified, and its results are anticipated to provide evidence for future updates to this review. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence available to guide decisions regarding the choice of surgical techniques for women with stage IA2 cervical cancer. The results of the ongoing randomized controlled trial are expected to enable comparisons between different surgical approaches in the future.
